Nic Dlamini and SANParks

By: Diana Lucas | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

Summary:
2020 was meant to be Nic Dlamini’s year, a possibility of representing South Africa at the Olympics and being the first black South African to be on the starting line of the Tour de France and then just a few days before the end of 2019 the altercation with SANParks officials on Table Mountain. An incident which went viral around the world on social media and left Dlamini with a broken humerus on an emergency operating table, putting his cycling career in jeopardy.

The video of Dlamini’s arrest showed SANParks rangers aggressively handling Dlamini and shoving him into the back of the van.

It took what happened to Nic to bring into the spotlight the situation on Table Mountain National Park, the incompetence and lack of training that many of the rangers have. There have many a many incidents and assaults going back at least six years, complaints have been ignored, reports to police swept under the carpet.

Further information:
The Cape Town branch of the Mountain Club of South Africa (MCSA) were inundated with complaints about rangers in the wake of this incident MCSA chairperson Martin Hutton-Squire, says that altercations between members of the public and park rangers appear to be far too common.

We will interview Shaun Sale who was pushed off the road whilst cycling on Silvermine 5.30 one evening, The ranger demanded to see his permit and told him too get off the mountain as it was too late, he was manhandled and pushed, there was a women in the bakkie which Shaun feels was the reason the ranger was behaving this way. Shaun pressed charges, nothing happened.

David Bland was roughed up in a very similar way. He was riding on the tar road of the Silvermine reserve, an bakkie ran him off the road and the ranger demanded to see his activity card
“ As the bakkie was unmarked and he had no identity markings on his clothing, I asked to see some form of identification to verify who he was so that I could report him for reckless driving. He then grabbed me by the throat and my immediate response was to defend myself which I did. We had an altercation and after a few fellow cyclist managed to stop the altercation, I mentioned to the ranger that I would be pressing assault charges against him . After mentioning this he proceeded to handcuff me and took me to Kirstenhof police station in the back of the unmarked bakkie where he pressed assault charges against me. Long story short, I finally managed to lay charges of assault against him at the police station as they refused to lay the charges against him.
This whole incident landed up in Wynberg court and after numerous appearances , the court clerk suggested I drop the charges and in turn he will get TMNP to drop their false charges.
As this was costing me a small fortune in lawyer’s fees, I agreed and dropped the charges and the case was closed,”



Pro-cyclist Matt Beers ( in the same league as Nic) suffered a similar assault whilst cycling.

Rens Rezelman: Chairman of the Pedal Power Association (PPA) one of the largest cycling clubs and most active on the mountain says it’s taken what happened to Nic to finally bring to wide attention what is happening. The rangers are not trained to deal with people, the PPA have offered to get involved to help train and mentor rangers, to maintain the cycle trails – another point the money that is gathered from hikers and cyclists and event to use the trail goes straight into national coffers and Rens says the tails are not well kept.

Rens was also part of the Cape Cycle Tour and has had dealing with SANParks, in that event as well. He says they are very greedy and demand huge amounts of money, money that does not get put back into keeping the mountain safe and cared for. For example the Cape Cycle Tour would pay around R70 0000 to place a water tank on a path (nowhere near flora and fauna) but that money doesn’t go towards keeping the mountain safe or maintained, the paths clean etc . It’s a huge shame as Cape Town is all about tourism – it is in effect a playground for tourists – of which cycling is one of the biggest draw cards and attract monied tourists. A great example of uplifting and mentoring communities is the Sani to Sea cycle race where the money is spent on hireing and training and uplifting communities to keep the natural areas clean and safe, this is what they wold like to see for Table Mountain National Park.

Martin Hutton-Squire says that when Table Mountain National Park was recognised in 1998 as a “urban park” it was agreed that it could not be administered in the same way that existing rural national parks were managed.
"An 'open access' urban park requires a particular approach to park management that is very different from what is relevant elsewhere. A resolution to the increasing conflict between the public, the rangers and park management will only be achieved once an 'independent review body'... has been established to consider the day-to-day management of the park, and once all the park rangers have been appropriately trained, given their very public role."
Stories of verbal insults and physical attacks to arrests and fines, it is clear that many park users have fallen victim to the poor training and unclear mandate of the rangers
We will talk to an ex ranger Alfredo Dixon, who will tell us about how rangers are just picked and put on the job, with no training and no expertise. He says there have been many more problems than we even know about, and some rangers have no clue how to do their job.

SANParks spokesperson Reynold Thakhuli has said he will not comment because of the ongoing investigation.
The five officials involved in the Dlamini incident have been officially suspended pending the outcome.

Press Release:


Cycling on Table Mountain
What was supposed to be pro cyclist Nic Dlamini’s year, as he worked to represent South Africa at the Olympics, has become a tough journey back to health as he nurses a broken arm, sustained in December when park rangers on Table Mountain assaulted him over his permit to ride. Carte Blanche asks how the country’s reputation can be restored in the face of ongoing complaints against park rangers.
Producer: Diana Lucas | Presenter: Derek Watts


Script:


Nic: It’s a phenomenal feeling just being able to start the Tour de France as the first black South African so obviously that’s meant a lot to me and the team as well.

VO
This year was going to be pro cyclist Nic Dlamini’s breakthrough year, with not only the possibility of being on the starting line of the world’s greatest cycle race but also representing South Africa at the Japan Olympics.

Nic: That’s my No 1 dream I’ve always wanted to do Olympics and represent South Africa and hopefully if I get back in time and feel strong I can be there.

V/0
But everything changed on one training ride.

Link: That’s the video that went viral when top cyclist Nic Dlamini was attacked by Park rangers here in the Silvermine area of the Cape late last year, the question being asked is was this an isolated incident or have some rangers gone rogue.

V/O
Nic has been advised by the legal firm representing him, Norton Rose Fulbright, not to talk about the incident.

Rens: I don’t like to look at it any more if you look at it closely you can hear the bone being broken. its inhumane.

V/O
Rens Rezelman is chairman of the Pedal Power Association or PPA an advocacy group for cyclists.

Derek: What have you pieced together about Nic’s incident?
Rens: Nic was busy training, the reason why its a good to train on the Silvermine stretch you get about 600 metres of vertical ascent which is difficult to find especially if you are wanting to race professionally in Europe and it looked like the rangers came along side him and demanded to see his permit… I’m then told he was pushed off bicycle but certainly from where the video clip picks up the interactions with the rangers is over the top aggressive and hostile, whether Nic had a permit to be there it’s irrelevant it’s a bit like saying I had a car license that had expired and I had parked in town and I got back and there were 5 metro cops with batons.

V/O
But what happened to Nic is not an isolated incident, the Mountain Club, Cape Town has been inundated with face book messages and e mails.
Shaun Sale was training on the same stretch of road as Nic.

Shaun: I was training along the contour path going up to Silvermine then coming back down on the tar road I was riding on the side of the road he swerved his vehicle into me I crashed into the bush the occupant jumped out it was a ranger by the time I worked it out he was grabbing me and shouting where’s your card?

Martin: If you go to Europe and you are a rock climber you just go and climb, if you come here and you start climbing in the wrong place you might get arrested.

V/O
Martin Hutton -Squire is Chairman of the Cape Town Section of the Mountain Club.
 
Martin: Table Mountain Park is totally unique in South Africa and much of the world because it’s in the middle of the city. We refer to it as Open Access Urban Park.

V/O
Table Mountain National Park stretches over 221 square kilometres. Every year over 2 and half million people visit it. It was in 1998 that SANParks or National Parks took control.

Martin: It was debated whether it should be Cape Nature from the province or the National Parks. One way or another it went to National Parks but the underlying agreement was that the Park belongs to citizens of Cape Town and of South Africa and it should be managed in such a way so available to everyone to use as an urban park, what’s happened it has become a cash cow for the South African National Parks
Derek: How many permits are there?
Martin: I actually don’t know, in the order of 60 or more. A friend of mine calculated that if he wanted to walk his dogs, cycle his bicycle; take his kids fishing on the beach and launch a small craft of the beach at Cape Point he would have to have 5 permits and cost in the region of 3 000 per annum. It actually means lots of people who live around Cape Town can never afford it.

Derek: So do Table Mountain National Park maintain the cycle trails?
Rens: No they don’t you would think that the amount of money we pay for an activity permit part of that at least would be allocated to maintaining trails but that is distinctly not the case.

V/O
But the1998 agreement states:
“ ….. the SANParks shall be solely responsible for the provision, maintenance and management of services and infrastructure within the park ……..”

Links: In another incident a young woman arrives from the UK and decides to enjoy the mountain area and cycle up to Rhodes memorial for a coffee …she’s found here in tears the rangers had apparently jumped out of their vehicle and harassed her for a permit

V/O
This was in February last year, it was cyclist John Wilkinson who came across this tourist in distress.

John Wilkinson She said that she had been stopped by three or four rangers they jumped out of their 4 X 4 and interrogated her for a level 3 activity permit. I thought she was on a road bike cycling up on the tar to café it should be absolutely fine anyway she decided not to carry on, so I was quiet angry at the time this is not the way to treat anyone let alone a tourist.

Martin: Table Mountain along with the beaches and the vineyards are the reason people come to Cape Town, but the average younger tourist wants to walk on the mountain they expect to be in a safe environment and to be welcomed…. if you are frightening away your tourists you are going to affect the economy of the Western Cape.

Rens: We have got events like the Cape Absa epic which brings to bear a huge amount of international tourists here. . …With the advent of e bikes we predict there will be more and more people coming here for bike tourism accessing points on the mountain they were unable to access.

V/O
In 2018, Carte Blanche investigated the high incidence of crime and opportunistic attacks on visitors to Table Mountain National Park.

Derek: Are the rangers responsible for our personal safety?
Martin: Lets be fair it is a very difficult thing to cope with when you have so many people close to the mountain but yes I would argue that they are responsible for our personal safety. There are some good people working on Table Mountain it’s just a group of rangers who are out of control,
Derek: Some of them gone rogue?
Martin: I think you’ve have to look at management and if management has got the wrong ethic and are putting across the wrong behavioral norms then you get things like this coming across.

V/O
Ex- SANPark ranger Alfredo Dixon agrees with Martin’s point, he was responsible for Health and Safety on the Mountain.

Alfredo: I feel SANParks is failing the rangers, because If some one don’t train you how are you going to know how to do it.
Derek: What training are you given when you join SANParks?
Alfredo: You did you fitness to check if you are fit, other then that you sign a contract, you get the uniform than you sent into the field. At the time some of the guys we employed were ex police and ex military but here were certain people was employed came from shoe shops and from factories who have no back ground with working with public.
Derek: Why did you leave?
Alfredo: I was fired because I exposed mismanagement in the Table Mountain National Park.
VO
Dixon openly posted on social media his views on the failings of SANPark management of Table Mountain National Park.
V/O
In a press statement SANParks said that Dixon was dismissed due to a failure to adhere to SANParks procedures in respect of social media engagements.

Link: People we should be speaking to are SANParks getting their side of the story, but they absolutely refused an on camera interview saying the matter is under investigation

V/ O
We replied saying we would not interview SANParks about the Nic Dlamini incident but there were other allegations about the management of Table Mountain National Park we wanted to raise with them.

Derek”
They replied ‘Unfortunately our decision stands we will not engage at the moment.’

Rens: SANParks find themselves in a position and certainly our experience over the years engaging with them does seem to be difficult their does seem to be a bit of a laager mentality. The cycling community brings with it many things of benefit to the Park.
We pay our way and I don’t think its asking too much just to expect some decency and humane and recognising that we bring a lot of economic activity to the city.

V/O
The five SANPark rangers involved in the Nic Dlemeni incident, were suspended pending the investigation…to date SANParks are not willing to comment further. For Nic he is determined to be back in the saddle.

Nic: God willing, I will be back in time.. you have to want to be there as well an keeping motivated to push now and be back on the bike as soon as possible getting back to where I was and sharpening up for the Tour de France and Olympics. I always say to myself I was born for greatness.

Nic: That’s my No 1 dream I’ve always wanted to do Olympics and represent South Africa and hopefully if I get back in time and feel strong I can be there. V/0 But everything changed on one training ride. Link: That’s the video that went viral when top cyclist Nic Dlamini was attacked by Park rangers here in the Silvermine area of the Cape late last year, the question being asked is was this an isolated incident or have some rangers gone rogue. V/O Nic has been advised by the legal firm representing him, Norton Rose Fulbright, not to talk about the incident. Rens: I don’t like to look at it any more if you look at it closely you can hear the bone being broken. its inhumane. V/O Rens Rezelman is chairman of the Pedal Power Association or PPA an advocacy group for cyclists. Derek: What have you pieced together about Nic’s incident? Rens: Nic was busy training, the reason why its a good to train on the Silvermine stretch you get about 600 metres of vertical ascent which is difficult to find especially if you are wanting to race professionally in Europe and it looked like the rangers came along side him and demanded to see his permit… I’m then told he was pushed off bicycle but certainly from where the video clip picks up the interactions with the rangers is over the top aggressive and hostile, whether Nic had a permit to be there it’s irrelevant it’s a bit like saying I had a car license that had expired and I had parked in town and I got back and there were 5 metro cops with batons. V/O But what happened to Nic is not an isolated incident, the Mountain Club, Cape Town has been inundated with face book messages and e mails. Shaun Sale was training on the same stretch of road as Nic. Shaun: I was training along the contour path going up to Silvermine then coming back down on the tar road I was riding on the side of the road he swerved his vehicle into me I crashed into the bush the occupant jumped out it was a ranger by the time I worked it out he was grabbing me and shouting where’s your card? Martin: If you go to Europe and you are a rock climber you just go and climb, if you come here and you start climbing in the wrong place you might get arrested. V/O Martin Hutton -Squire is Chairman of the Cape Town Section of the Mountain Club. Martin: Table Mountain Park is totally unique in South Africa and much of the world because it’s in the middle of the city. We refer to it as Open Access Urban Park. V/O Table Mountain National Park stretches over 221 square kilometres. Every year over 2 and half million people visit it. It was in 1998 that SANParks or National Parks took control. Martin: It was debated whether it should be Cape Nature from the province or the National Parks. One way or another it went to National Parks but the underlying agreement was that the Park belongs to citizens of Cape Town and of South Africa and it should be managed in such a way so available to everyone to use as an urban park, what’s happened it has become a cash cow for the South African National Parks Derek: How many permits are there? Martin: I actually don’t know, in the order of 60 or more. A friend of mine calculated that if he wanted to walk his dogs, cycle his bicycle; take his kids fishing on the beach and launch a small craft of the beach at Cape Point he would have to have 5 permits and cost in the region of 3 000 per annum. It actually means lots of people who live around Cape Town can never afford it. Derek: So do Table Mountain National Park maintain the cycle trails? Rens: No they don’t you would think that the amount of money we pay for an activity permit part of that at least would be allocated to maintaining trails but that is distinctly not the case. V/O But the1998 agreement states: “ ….. the SANParks shall be solely responsible for the provision, maintenance and management of services and infrastructure within the park ……..” Links: In another incident a young woman arrives from the UK and decides to enjoy the mountain area and cycle up to Rhodes memorial for a coffee …she’s found here in tears the rangers had apparently jumped out of their vehicle and harassed her for a permit V/O This was in February last year, it was cyclist John Wilkinson who came across this tourist in distress. John Wilkinson She said that she had been stopped by three or four rangers they jumped out of their 4 X 4 and interrogated her for a level 3 activity permit. I thought she was on a road bike cycling up on the tar to café it should be absolutely fine anyway she decided not to carry on, so I was quiet angry at the time this is not the way to treat anyone let alone a tourist. Martin: Table Mountain along with the beaches and the vineyards are the reason people come to Cape Town, but the average younger tourist wants to walk on the mountain they expect to be in a safe environment and to be welcomed…. if you are frightening away your tourists you are going to affect the economy of the Western Cape. Rens: We have got events like the Cape Absa epic which brings to bear a huge amount of international tourists here. . …With the advent of e bikes we predict there will be more and more people coming here for bike tourism accessing points on the mountain they were unable to access. V/O In 2018, Carte Blanche investigated the high incidence of crime and opportunistic attacks on visitors to Table Mountain National Park. Derek: Are the rangers responsible for our personal safety? Martin: Lets be fair it is a very difficult thing to cope with when you have so many people close to the mountain but yes I would argue that they are responsible for our personal safety. There are some good people working on Table Mountain it’s just a group of rangers who are out of control, Derek: Some of them gone rogue? Martin: I think you’ve have to look at management and if management has got the wrong ethic and are putting across the wrong behavioral norms then you get things like this coming across. V/O Ex- SANPark ranger Alfredo Dixon agrees with Martin’s point, he was responsible for Health and Safety on the Mountain. Alfredo: I feel SANParks is failing the rangers, because If some one don’t train you how are you going to know how to do it. Derek: What training are you given when you join SANParks? Alfredo: You did you fitness to check if you are fit, other then that you sign a contract, you get the uniform than you sent into the field. At the time some of the guys we employed were ex police and ex military but here were certain people was employed came from shoe shops and from factories who have no back ground with working with public. Derek: Why did you leave? Alfredo: I was fired because I exposed mismanagement in the Table Mountain National Park. VO Dixon openly posted on social media his views on the failings of SANPark management of Table Mountain National Park. V/O In a press statement SANParks said that Dixon was dismissed due to a failure to adhere to SANParks procedures in respect of social media engagements. Link: People we should be speaking to are SANParks getting their side of the story, but they absolutely refused an on camera interview saying the matter is under investigation V/ O We replied saying we would not interview SANParks about the Nic Dlamini incident but there were other allegations about the management of Table Mountain National Park we wanted to raise with them. Derek” They replied ‘Unfortunately our decision stands we will not engage at the moment.’ Rens: SANParks find themselves in a position and certainly our experience over the years engaging with them does seem to be difficult their does seem to be a bit of a laager mentality. The cycling community brings with it many things of benefit to the Park. We pay our way and I don’t think its asking too much just to expect some decency and humane and recognising that we bring a lot of economic activity to the city. V/O The five SANPark rangers involved in the Nic Dlemeni incident, were suspended pending the investigation…to date SANParks are not willing to comment further. For Nic he is determined to be back in the saddle. Nic: God willing, I will be back in time.. you have to want to be there as well an keeping motivated to push now and be back on the bike as soon as possible getting back to where I was and sharpening up for the Tour de France and Olympics. I always say to myself I was born for greatness.

metadata.Summary: 2020 was meant to be Nic Dlamini’s year, a possibility of representing South Africa at the Olympics and being the first black South African to be on the starting line of the Tour de France and then just a few days before the end of 2019 the altercation with SANParks officials on Table Mountain. An incident which went viral around the world on social media and left Dlamini with a broken humerus on an emergency operating table, putting his cycling career in jeopardy. The video of Dlamini’s arrest showed SANParks rangers aggressively handling Dlamini and shoving him into the back of the van. It took what happened to Nic to bring into the spotlight the situation on Table Mountain National Park, the incompetence and lack of training that many of the rangers have. There have many a many incidents and assaults going back at least six years, complaints have been ignored, reports to police swept under the carpet.
metadata.Further information: The Cape Town branch of the Mountain Club of South Africa (MCSA) were inundated with complaints about rangers in the wake of this incident MCSA chairperson Martin Hutton-Squire, says that altercations between members of the public and park rangers appear to be far too common. We will interview Shaun Sale who was pushed off the road whilst cycling on Silvermine 5.30 one evening, The ranger demanded to see his permit and told him too get off the mountain as it was too late, he was manhandled and pushed, there was a women in the bakkie which Shaun feels was the reason the ranger was behaving this way. Shaun pressed charges, nothing happened. David Bland was roughed up in a very similar way. He was riding on the tar road of the Silvermine reserve, an bakkie ran him off the road and the ranger demanded to see his activity card “ As the bakkie was unmarked and he had no identity markings on his clothing, I asked to see some form of identification to verify who he was so that I could report him for reckless driving. He then grabbed me by the throat and my immediate response was to defend myself which I did. We had an altercation and after a few fellow cyclist managed to stop the altercation, I mentioned to the ranger that I would be pressing assault charges against him . After mentioning this he proceeded to handcuff me and took me to Kirstenhof police station in the back of the unmarked bakkie where he pressed assault charges against me. Long story short, I finally managed to lay charges of assault against him at the police station as they refused to lay the charges against him. This whole incident landed up in Wynberg court and after numerous appearances , the court clerk suggested I drop the charges and in turn he will get TMNP to drop their false charges. As this was costing me a small fortune in lawyer’s fees, I agreed and dropped the charges and the case was closed,” Pro-cyclist Matt Beers ( in the same league as Nic) suffered a similar assault whilst cycling. Rens Rezelman: Chairman of the Pedal Power Association (PPA) one of the largest cycling clubs and most active on the mountain says it’s taken what happened to Nic to finally bring to wide attention what is happening. The rangers are not trained to deal with people, the PPA have offered to get involved to help train and mentor rangers, to maintain the cycle trails – another point the money that is gathered from hikers and cyclists and event to use the trail goes straight into national coffers and Rens says the tails are not well kept. Rens was also part of the Cape Cycle Tour and has had dealing with SANParks, in that event as well. He says they are very greedy and demand huge amounts of money, money that does not get put back into keeping the mountain safe and cared for. For example the Cape Cycle Tour would pay around R70 0000 to place a water tank on a path (nowhere near flora and fauna) but that money doesn’t go towards keeping the mountain safe or maintained, the paths clean etc . It’s a huge shame as Cape Town is all about tourism – it is in effect a playground for tourists – of which cycling is one of the biggest draw cards and attract monied tourists. A great example of uplifting and mentoring communities is the Sani to Sea cycle race where the money is spent on hireing and training and uplifting communities to keep the natural areas clean and safe, this is what they wold like to see for Table Mountain National Park. Martin Hutton-Squire says that when Table Mountain National Park was recognised in 1998 as a “urban park” it was agreed that it could not be administered in the same way that existing rural national parks were managed. "An 'open access' urban park requires a particular approach to park management that is very different from what is relevant elsewhere. A resolution to the increasing conflict between the public, the rangers and park management will only be achieved once an 'independent review body'... has been established to consider the day-to-day management of the park, and once all the park rangers have been appropriately trained, given their very public role." Stories of verbal insults and physical attacks to arrests and fines, it is clear that many park users have fallen victim to the poor training and unclear mandate of the rangers We will talk to an ex ranger Alfredo Dixon, who will tell us about how rangers are just picked and put on the job, with no training and no expertise. He says there have been many more problems than we even know about, and some rangers have no clue how to do their job. SANParks spokesperson Reynold Thakhuli has said he will not comment because of the ongoing investigation. The five officials involved in the Dlamini incident have been officially suspended pending the outcome.
